analysis.one_liner: Lets small employers and self-employed people band together to buy health plans exempt from some Affordable Care Act rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died at the end of the 117th Congress, with 8 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law rules letting groups of small employers and self-employed people sponsor association health plans, and would let short-term, limited-duration insurance plans last up to a year. Those plans are exempt from some Affordable Care Act market rules, including protections for people with preexisting conditions. It would also codify a 2018 Trump administration rule that a federal judge threw out in 2019. The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Small business owners and self-employed people, especially healthy ones, who could band together and buy coverage at lower premiums than individual ACA plans. Health insurers and business associations gain a new pool of customers selling plans that don't have to meet all ACA requirements. Franchise chains gain a shield: the bill says sponsoring or facilitating such a plan cannot establish a joint employer relationship, limiting their liability to franchisee workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small business owners, self-employed people, and insurers

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets groups of employers in the same trade, industry, or region sponsor a group health plan as if they were a single large employer, which supporters say lets small businesses use their combined buying power to get lower premiums.

Self-employed 'working owners' who work at least 20 hours a week or earn at least the cost of their coverage could qualify as both employer and employee, giving solo entrepreneurs access to group-style coverage.
The bill would allow short-term, limited-duration plans to cover a period of less than 12 months, a cheaper option for people who can pass underwriting.

The bill includes nondiscrimination requirements: association plans could not deny membership or set premiums based on health factors within the association, and plans could not be owned or controlled by an insurer.

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions and expensive health needs, in two ways: association and short-term plans are exempt from some ACA market rules, so sicker people who stay in ACA-compliant plans face higher premiums as healthier enrollees leave those pools, and anyone buying the cheaper plans risks coverage that pays for less than expected. Enrollees in an association plan also bear the risk if the association or the plan becomes insolvent. Workers at franchises lose the joint-employer protection the bill shields franchisors from.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and ACA enrollees

drawbacks.text: Short-term, limited-duration plans are exempt from ACA market requirements such as coverage of individuals with preexisting conditions, so the cheaper plans can deny or price out people who are sick and can cover less care.
A federal district judge vacated the 2018 Labor Department rule that this bill would restore, finding it unlawful; the bill would recreate by statute the arrangement a court struck down.

The bill bars any federal or state law from treating participation in an association plan as creating an employer or joint-employer relationship, including for franchisors and franchisees — a liability shield that weakens workers' ability to hold the parent company responsible.
ACA-compliant individual and small-group markets could lose healthier, cheaper-to-insure enrollees, raising premiums for those who remain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real benefit: some small employers and self-employed people would genuinely pay less for coverage, and the bill carries its own nondiscrimination rules. But the savings come largely from skimming healthier people into plans that don't have to meet ACA standards, which raises costs and narrows protections for the people who need coverage most — and association plans have a history of leaving enrollees stranded when they fail. On balance the bill trades broad consumer protections for cheaper options for a narrower, healthier group.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the Association Health Plans Act of 2021 on July 20, 2021, joined by 8 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill would have codified rules from the Labor Department's June 2018 final rule expanding association health plans, which a federal district judge vacated on March 28, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on ACA protections, especially those with preexisting conditions, keep the stronger rulebook, and insurers do not gain the lighter-regulated association and short-term plan markets the bill would have opened. Small business owners and self-employed people looking for cheaper group coverage do not get it either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on ACA protections; insurers lose the market

for.name: Rep. Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set out its case: association plans already produced premium decreases of up to 29 percent for small business owners and are governed by the same consumer protections as large employer plans.

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, so it never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 supporters (the sponsor plus 8 cosponsors) were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without any action.

industries.note: The bill would open a large market for association and short-term plans that are exempt from some ACA market rules, letting insurers sell cheaper, thinner coverage. The profit comes from plans that can cover less and exclude sicker buyers, a cost shifted onto ACA-compliant pools and people with health needs.

Business associations could sponsor plans for members, and the bill says facilitating an association plan cannot create a joint-employer relationship under any federal or state law — shielding franchisors from liability to franchisee workers. That is a liability benefit separate from the health coverage itself.

industries.industry: Small business owners and self-employed people
industries.note: Healthy small employers and self-employed working owners would gain access to lower-premium group coverage. The benefit applies mainly to those who can pass underwriting; it comes partly at the expense of people left in the ACA-compliant market.
